About This Simulation

⚛ Physics

A Gaussian wave packet evolving under the free-particle Schrödinger equation, built from a superposition of plane waves with different momenta.

  • Dispersion: Each momentum component k travels at phase velocity ω/k = k, causing the packet to spread over time
  • Wave function: ψ(x,t) = Σ cₖ exp(ikx − iωt) where ω = k²
  • Spreading: Width grows as σ(t) = σ₀√(1 + t²/σ₀⁴) — narrower packets spread faster

🎨 Visuals

  • Top panel: Individual Fourier modes with rotating phasors showing phase evolution e^{−iωt}
  • Bottom panel: The coherent sum — |ψ|² (probability density), Re[ψ], Im[ψ]
  • Dashed gray: Initial |ψ₀|² for comparison
  • Gold line: Classical particle position (group velocity)

🎮 Controls

  • σ — Initial width (smaller = faster spreading)
  • x₀ — Starting position of the wave packet
  • N — Number of Fourier modes to display
  • Speed — Animation playback rate
  • Show Real/Imag — Toggle visibility of Re[ψ] and Im[ψ]

Guided Inquiry

1 · A packet made of plane waves

Here’s the idea. On the circle −π ≤ x ≤ π, a Gaussian packet is written as a sum of plane waves with whole-number k, each carrying its own amplitude |c| and phase. The upper row shows you three of those waves — amplitude, turning phase, and the wave itself. The plot below is their sum |ψ|², drawn against the dashed Gaussian they’re building.

2 · Spreading in x, spreading in k?

Let’s start the clock. As time runs, the probability curve begins to change shape. What do you think the amplitude |c| of each plane wave will do as that happens?

3 · How fast each phase turns

Now watch the phases. The k = 0 wave stands still, while k = +1 and k = −1 turn together. Taken over all k, how do you think the turning rate goes?

4 · Off the circle

Now for a bigger question. Here x wraps around a circle, so only whole-number k occur, and at t = 2π every phase has turned a whole number of times — the packet returns exactly as it began. A free particle on an infinite line carries every real k, under the same rate law. What do you think happens to its packet?

5 · A wider packet

One last experiment. The packet is now rebuilt four times wider in x, at σ = 1.0, with the same seven waves shown. What do you think building a wider packet in x calls for?

The Physics

A wave packet on a ring · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim builds a localised wave packet on a ring out of plane waves with whole-number k, then lets the clock run, in units where ħ = 2m = 1. It shows how the packet's shape comes from the amplitudes and phases of its waves, and so how a free quantum particle's wave function changes with time.

What you'll learn

  • How a packet is a sum of plane waves, and how many of them you must draw to reproduce it.
  • How the packet's width in x is tied to the range of k it contains.
  • What time does to each wave, and how that reshapes the packet.
  • When the packet returns to its starting shape, and what sets that time.
Plane waves of different whole-number k add up to a hump, drawn against a fixed dashed target.

What's on screen

  • Cards across the top, one per wave drawn: its k, its amplitude |c|, an arrow for its phase, and the wave itself.
  • Fourier Sum |ψ|² (white): the probability density of the waves you draw, with the real and imaginary parts of ψ in lime and rose.
  • Target Gaussian |ψ|² (dashed slate): the packet at t = 0 built from all 80 waves. It never changes.
  • Statistics: the clock t, Total Norm, Plotted Norm and Captured. The ⟳ FULL REVIVAL badge in the top bar lights near t = 2π.
See itDraw just three waves, k = −1, 0, +1. Watch for: the white curve lower and broader than the dashed target, with Captured well below 100%.

03

A packet is a sum of waves

On the ring only plane waves with whole-number k fit. Any packet can be written as a sum of them, with one complex number ck per wave: |ck| is the wave's amplitude and the phase of ck sets where along x it starts.

One number per plane wave. That is all a Fourier decomposition is.

The sim draws only the N waves with the largest |ck| and adds them. Captured is the share of the packet's probability, Σ|ck|², that those N waves carry.

The white curve is |ψN|². Captured counts what it contains.
  • |ψ|² is a probability density. Over the whole ring it integrates to 1 (Total Norm).
  • The dashed target is the t = 0 packet built from all 80 waves. At σ = 0.25, N = 3 captures about 55% of it and N = 13 about 99.9%.
See itAt σ = 0.25, add waves in steps: N = 3, 5, 7, then 13. Watch for: the white curve growing toward the dashed target as Captured climbs.
04

Narrow in x, wide in k

The sim's packet is a Gaussian, ψ(x, 0) ∝ exp[−(x − x₀)²/4σ²]. Its amplitudes are a Gaussian too, |ck| ∝ e−k²σ², so the two widths are tied together:

  • Δx = σ, the rms width of |ψ|².
  • Δk = 1/2σ, the rms width of |ck|².
  • Δx·Δk = ½, the smallest product the uncertainty relation allows (Δp = ħΔk).
The packet in x and in k at t = 0, σ = 0.25: narrow in x, wide in k.

Halving σ doubles Δk, so a narrower packet needs waves out to larger |k|. A wider packet needs fewer: at σ = 1.0 the three waves k = 0, ±1 carry over 99%, against about 55% at σ = 0.25.

At the widest settings the ring cuts the Gaussian's tails and the sim wraps them round, so σ is then the Gaussian's parameter rather than a measured width.

See itDraw the same three waves at σ = 0.25, then at σ = 1.0. Watch for: the 3-wave curve missing the dashed target at σ = 0.25 and lying on it at σ = 1.0.
05

Time turns each wave's phase

Each wave k has energy E = ħ²k²/2m, which is k² with ħ = 2m = 1, so its phase turns at the angular frequency ωk = k²:

The amplitudes are frozen. Time only touches the phase of each wave.
  • Every |ck| stays fixed. Only the phases turn: k = 0 stands still, k = ±1 turn together, k = ±2 turn four times faster, k = ±3 nine times faster.
  • |ψ|² changes because the waves drift out of step. Re ψ and Im ψ hold the phase information that |ψ|² hides: at t = 0 the packet is real, so Im ψ starts flat.
  • The amber dashed line vg marks x₀ + vgt, where vg = dω/dk = 2k at the packet's mean k. That mean is 0 here, so the line stays at x₀.
See itDraw seven waves, k = −3 … 3, and run the clock from 0. Watch for: the k = ±3 arrows whirling, k = ±1 turning slowly, k = 0 not at all, and every |c| unchanged.
06

Why the packet spreads

Waves with large |k| turn fastest, so they fall out of step with the slow ones. For a free particle on a line the Gaussian's width then grows as

The free-particle spreading law, and the time τ at which the width has grown by √2.
  • At t = τ = σ₀² the width is √2 larger and the peak of |ψ|² is √2 lower. Total probability stays 1; it is spread over more of x.
  • A narrower packet has a larger Δk, so it spreads sooner: halve σ₀ and τ is four times shorter.
  • On the ring this law holds only until the packet meets itself. At σ₀ = 0.25 that is about t = 0.45, when the law's width reaches π/√3 ≈ 1.81, the width of probability spread evenly round the ring.
σ N

These sliders move the sim too. Changing σ restarts the clock at t = 0.

See itRun from t = 0 at σ = 0.25 with N = 13, and pause at t = τ and again at t = 0.45. Watch for: the white peak falling to about 0.7 of the dashed height by t = τ, then a low ripple spread round the whole ring.
07

The packet returns on a ring

On the ring every k is a whole number, so every turning rate k² is too. After t = 2π, wave k has turned exactly k² times and all the phases are back together. At t = π the factor e−ik²π equals (−1)k, which is what shifting x by π does to eikx.

Every turning rate is a whole number, so every phase returns together.
  • t = 2π: the packet is exactly as it began.
  • t = π: the same packet, on the opposite side of the ring.
  • t = π/2: two copies, at x₀ and x₀ + π, each carrying half the probability.
The sim's own |ψ|² at four times, drawn from its 80 coefficients.

The ⟳ badge lights for t within 0.3 of a multiple of 2π, so it also lights just after a restart at t = 0. That is the start, not a revival.

See itStart the packet at x₀ = 1.5 with N = 13 and pause at t = π, then run on to t = 2π. Watch for: the packet reappearing on the far side of the ring at t/2π = 0.5, then back on the dashed curve at 1.0.
08

Where it matters

  • A free electron spreads almost at once. In real units τ = 2mσ₀²/ħ. For σ₀ = 1 nm that is about 1.7 × 10⁻¹⁴ s, and the width has doubled by about 3 × 10⁻¹⁴ s.
  • A heavy object barely spreads at all. A 1 g bead with σ₀ = 1 µm has τ of about 2 × 10¹⁹ s, roughly forty times the age of the universe.
  • Spreading and revival are seen in experiments. Wave packets of highly excited (Rydberg) atoms spread and later come back, fully or in fractions, approximately.
Go deeper: units and the revival time
  • On a ring of radius R the energies are Ek = ħ²k²/2mR². With R = 1 and ħ = 2m = 1 this is k², and the revival time 2π becomes T = 4πmR²/ħ. For an electron on a ring of radius 1 nm, T ≈ 1.1 × 10⁻¹³ s.
  • The same arithmetic describes light passing a periodic grating: copies of the pattern, and fractional copies, reappear at fixed distances (the Talbot effect).
09

Summary

In one line. A packet on a ring is a sum of waves with fixed amplitudes. Free evolution only turns their phases, at rates k², which spreads the packet and, because k is a whole number, returns it at t = 2π.

Key points

  • ψ = Σ ck eikx; |ψ|² is a density that integrates to 1.
  • Δx = σ, Δk = 1/2σ, Δx·Δk = ½: narrow in x means wide in k.
  • Each |ck| stays fixed; wave k's phase turns at ω = k² (ħ = 2m = 1).
  • The width grows by √2 at τ = σ₀². On the ring the packet returns at 2π, shifted at π, in two halves at π/2.

Common mix-ups

  • "The packet spreads because each wave spreads." Each wave already fills the ring and its amplitude never changes. The phases drift out of step.
  • "The packet loses probability as it spreads." Total Norm stays 1; the same probability covers more of x.
  • "Captured says how accurate the physics is." It says how much of the packet the N chosen waves draw. Those waves evolve exactly.

Things to try on your own

  • At σ = 0.25, find the smallest N with Captured above 99%. Repeat at σ = 0.5.
  • Set x₀ = −2, pause near t/2π = 0.5, and read off where the packet sits.
  • Hide Re ψ, keep Im ψ, and describe it at t = 0 and a little later.
